abstract: "Understanding the factors associated with large fire perimeters is important for operational response and wildfire planning. This paper considers 8,476 California Wildfire Perimeters between 2000 and 2025, and employs simple linear regression to investigate the relationship between time to contain the fire and total burnt area. From this model, it was found that there was a significant positive correlation between the predictor and response variables; but only 24.57% of the variation in the log transformed acres was explained. These results indicate that other variables also influence the total area burned and that containment duration alone is not enough to accurately predict a fire’s final size.\n"

# Introduction

Most of the highly destructive fires in California have been reported in the past two decades. This includes the 2018 Camp Fire, the worst wildfire in the state’s history that caused massive loss of life, as well as the 2025 Palisades and Eaton Fires, which broke out without warning and lasted for a month. These increasingly recent record-breaking fires highlight the severe wildfire impacts that can occur when fires burn over a sustained period of time.

In addition to emergency response, continuous monitoring of fire spread is essential for firefighting systems. These systems are implemented as counteractive measures to reduce the spread of ignitions. Using data from previous fires is very important in the pursuit of estimating total fire damage and total area burned. Firefighters are known to react to immediate dangers and on-site activities; nevertheless, because of the advances in technologies like satellite imaging, radar, and forecasting, we can now gain a clearer picture of the damage caused by fires.

Several studies have used complex physical simulations to evaluate the spread of fires and estimate total damage [1-3]. However, these simulations are often computationally expensive and time-consuming. Machine Learning techniques such as linear regression, allow for much faster analysis of wildfires, by learning from historical data of past fires to interpret the behavior of future fires. This paper uses linear regression to observe how large past fires have gotten as a result of the time it took to contain them. More specifically we ask: Is time to containment associated with the total area burned by California wildfires recorded from 2000 through 2025? This will provide important information to entities such as utility companies, insurance companies, and public sectors, which can aide in preparation for rebuilding.

The paper is organized as follows. We start by presenting the collected data, outlier observations, and methods of regression analysis. Then, we present the fitted model and lay out the comparison metrics. Finally, we examine the results and interpret how this model could help inform operational responses to wildfires.

# Data

The dataset used in this project reports fire perimeters within California, as reported by the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection's Fire and Resource Assessment Program (FRAP) [4]. Each observation is a mapped fire perimeter. This dataset is updated annually and contains mapped wildfire perimeters collected by CAL FIRE and cooperating agencies, including the United States Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, California State Parks, National Park Service, and United States Fish and Wildlife Service. The complete dataset includes records of fires as far back as 1878. For the model, we will filter the data to only California fire records from 2000 through 2025. 

The response variable we are looking at is the recorded fire perimeter, measured as GIS-Calculated Acres, which strictly valued as estimated land area contain within the mapped fire perimeter. The predictor variable is time to containment, calculated as the number of days from the start of the alarm date to the end of the containment date. Under this definition, fires contained on the same calendar day they were reported, have a duration of one day. It is important to note that this measurement does not represent the exact elapsed time in hours, but rather the number of calendar days spanned by the fire.

Cleaning this dataset is important because there are instances of missing observations, such as those without a recorded alarm or containment date. In addition, this dataset reports fires of all sizes, both large and small, including those that were contained on the same calendar day. After cleaning, the final dataset contained 8,476 fire perimeters. Of these observations, 3,891 had an alarm and containment date on the same calendar day and were therefore assigned a containment duration of one day.

```{r data-cleaning, results='hide'}
data <- read.csv("./fire.csv")

# Convert dates
data$Alarm.Date <- as.Date(
  data$Alarm.Date,
  format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p"
)

data$Containment.Date <- as.Date(
  data$Containment.Date,
  format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p"
)

# Keep usable California fires from 2000 through 2025
fire <- subset(
  data,
  State == "CA" &
    Year >= 2000 &
    Year <= 2025 &
    !is.na(Alarm.Date) &
    !is.na(Containment.Date) &
    !is.na(GIS.Calculated.Acres) &
    GIS.Calculated.Acres > 0
)

# Calculate calendar-day differences
fire$Duration <- as.numeric(
  fire$Containment.Date - fire$Alarm.Date
)

# Remove impossible negative durations
fire <- subset(fire, Duration >= 0)

# Count the alarm date as Day 1
fire$Duration <- fire$Duration + 1

# Create log-transformed variables
fire$Log.Acres <- log(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres)
fire$Log.Duration <- log(fire$Duration)
```

```{r table-one}
table1 <- data.frame(
  Variable = c(
    "Time to containment (days)",
    "GIS-calculated acres"
  ),
  Observations = c(
    length(fire$Duration),
    length(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres)
  ),
  Mean = round(c(
    mean(fire$Duration),
    mean(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres)
  ), 2),
  SD = round(c(
    sd(fire$Duration),
    sd(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres)
  ), 2),
  Median = round(c(
    median(fire$Duration),
    median(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres)
  ), 2),
  Minimum = c(
    as.character(min(fire$Duration)),
    formatC(
      min(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres),
      format = "e",
      digits = 2
    )
  ),
  Maximum = round(c(
    max(fire$Duration),
    max(fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres)
  ), 2)
)

knitr::kable(
  table1,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Summary statistics for time to containment and GIS-calculated acres."
)
```

Table 1 provides the distribution of the data. We can see how heavily skewed the fire perimeter data are. With a mean of 2,489.34 acres and a median of 41.60 acres, the data are very heavily right-skewed. This provides evidence for the use of a logarithmic transformation of GIS-calculated acres as the response variable for linear regression.

Figure 1 compares the distributions of untransformed time to containment and GIS-calculated acreage. Both distributions are extremely right-skewed, with most fires being contained within a relatively short period of time and burning relatively small areas. However, a small number of fires experienced substantially longer containment durations and burned significantly larger areas, producing long right tails in both distributions.


```{r raw-distributions, fig.cap="Distributions of untransformed time to containment (days) and GIS-calculated acreage for California wildfires.", fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Time to containment
hist(
  fire$Duration,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Distribution of Time to Containment",
  xlab = "Time to Containment (Days)"
)

# (c) Acres burned
hist(
  fire$GIS.Calculated.Acres,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Distribution of Acres Burned",
  xlab = "GIS-Calculated Acres"
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

Therefore, I looked to transform the data to reduce the skewness of both distributions using logarithmic transformations. I decided to use the natural logarithm of the inclusive time to containment and the natural logarithm of GIS-calculated acreage. After these transformations, the extreme values were compressed, and the distribution of acreage became substantially more symmetric. However, time to containment remained heavily right-skewed due to the large number of fires contained on the same calendar day. The distributions of the log-transformed predictor and response variables can be seen below in Figure 2.

```{r acreage-distributions, fig.cap="Distributions of log-transformed GIS-calculated acreage and log-transformed time to containment for California wildfires.", fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Log time to containment
hist(
  fire$Log.Duration,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Distribution of Log Time",
  xlab = "Log(Time to Containment)"
)


# Log acres burned
hist(
  fire$Log.Acres,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Distribution of Log Acres",
  xlab = "Log GIS-Calculated Acres"
)


par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the data. First, this dataset does not contain every single wildfire in California's history, as some historical records were lost or insufficiently documented. However, the largest and most impactful fires have been accurately documented and rigorously verified. Collection methods can also vary among reporting agencies, potentially introducing inconsistencies in the data. Additionally, some fire perimeters were recorded to be under one acre, resulting in negative log values. This can be seen in the distribution of log acres, where the bottom tail extends into the negative region. Because all acreage measurements were positive, these observations were retained. Another limitation is that this analysis focuses on time as the only predictor variable, although other variables, such as weather, fuel moisture, and topography, have been shown to play a significant role in fire perimeter area. Furthermore, several developments in fire containment measures and environmental conditions have occurred over the 25 years of the study. Advancements in early detection, satellite imagery, and firefighting equipment might have played some role in the time taken to contain fires. At the same time, global warming has contributed to warmer and drier environmental conditions, increasing the possibility of bigger and fiercer fires.

# Methods

Simple linear regression was used to examine the association between time to containment and total area burned by California wildfires. Let \(Y_i\) represent the GIS-calculated acreage for fire perimeter \(i\), and let \(X_i\) represent the number of days between the start of its alarm date and and end of containment dates. The final regression model was

\[
\log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log(X_i) + \varepsilon_i,
\]

where \(\beta_0\) is the expected log acreage when a fire has a recorded containment duration of one day, \(\beta_1\) represents the association between containment duration and acreage, and \(\varepsilon_i\) is the random error for observation \(i\). The errors were assumed to have a mean of zero, constant variance \(\sigma^2\), and to be independent across observations.

At first, a linear regression model was anticipated to be fitted to the untransformed data; however, with the strongly right-skewed distributions, it was apparent that the relationship would not appear to be linear. The use of the natural logarithm of acreage was necessary to properly fit the model to the response variable. The predictor was transformed using the natural logarithm of time to containment.Since the minimum value of time to containment is one day, the logarithmic transformation can be applied directly without excluding any observations. These transformations allowed for accounting for outlier fires and helped p roduce a more linear relationship between the predictor and response. Because both variables were transformed, \(\beta_1\) can be interpreted as the approximate percentage change in acreage associated with a 1% increase in \(X_i\).

The model parameters were estimated using ordinary least squares. This method chooses estimates \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) that minimize the sum of the squared residuals,

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
\log(Y_i)-\left\{b_0+b_1\log(X_i)\right\}
\right]^2.
\]

A two-sided hypothesis test was used to test

\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
H_A:\beta_1\neq0.
\]

A 95% confidence interval was also constructed for \(\beta_1\). Model fit was summarized using \(R^2\), which represents the proportion of variation in log acreage explained by log-transformed containment duration, and the residual standard error.

Several assumptions must be satisfied for the hypothesis test and 95% confidence interval to be statistically valid under the standard linear regression model. These include the validity of the data for the research question, the representativeness of our sample compared to the population of California wildfires, additivity and linearity of the relationship after the log transformations, independence of errors across observations, equal error variance, and normality of errors. To assess these assumptions, a scatterplot of the transformed variables and a residual-versus-fitted plot were used to examine how linear the relationship appeared to be. The residual plot was also used to evaluate whether the errors had constant variance and to identify unusual observations. A normal Q–Q plot was used to evaluate the normality of the residuals. The validity and representativeness of the data, along with the independence assumption, were considered based on the characteristics of the dataset and how the observations were collected. Together, these evaluations helped identify improvements in linearity after the log transformations and remaining departures from the equal variance and normality assumptions.

All data cleaning, model fitting, tables, and figures were completed in R, and the simple linear regression model was fitted using the `lm()` function.

```{r fit-model, results='hide'}
model <- lm(Log.Acres ~ Log.Duration, data = fire)
```

# Results

Our results display a positive relationship between our predictor variable and the response variable. As seen in Figure 3, the relationship between log-transformed time to containment and log-transformed acreage shows a positive relationship with substantial variation around the fitted line. It is apparent that fires with similar containment durations could sometimes have considerably different burned areas, indicating that containment duration alone cannot fully explain fire sizes.

```{r duration-and-acreage, fig.cap="Log-transformed time to containment and log-transformed acreage, with the fitted regression line.", fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
plot(
  fire$Log.Duration,
  fire$Log.Acres,
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.4,
  col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.2),
  xlab = "Log(Time to Containment)",
  ylab = "Log GIS-Calculated Acres",
  main = "Containment Duration and Area Burned"
)

abline(model, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```



The fitted regression equation is shown in Table 2 and is

\[
\widehat{\log(Y_i)} = 2.8688 + 1.0206\log(X_i),
\]

where \(Y_i\) is GIS-calculated acreage and \(X_i\) is time to containment in days.

```{r table-two}
coefficients <- summary(model)$coefficients
confidence_intervals <- confint(model)

table2 <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Intercept", "Log(Duration)"),
  Estimate = round(coefficients[, "Estimate"], 4),
  `Standard Error` = round(coefficients[, "Std. Error"], 4),
  `t-value` = round(coefficients[, "t value"], 2),
  `95% Confidence Interval` = paste0(
    "(",
    round(confidence_intervals[, 1], 4),
    ", ",
    round(confidence_intervals[, 2], 4),
    ")"
  ),
  `p-value` = format.pval(
    coefficients[, "Pr(>|t|)"],
    digits = 3,
    eps = 0.001
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  table2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Estimated coefficients for the simple linear regression model."
)
```

We see that the slope has a p-value under 0.05, so we reject (H_0:\beta_1=0) and conclude that there is sufficient evidence of a positive association between containment duration and area burned. The estimated slope indicates that a 1% increase in \(X_i\) was associated with an approximately 1.02% increase in predicted area burned. The intercept indicates that a fire with a recorded duration of one day had a predicted log acreage of 2.8688, or about 17.6 acres. Furthermore, the model had an \(R^2\) value of 0.2457, meaning that approximately 24.57% of the variation in log acreage was explained by log-transformed containment duration. The remaining 75.43% was not explained by the model and may reflect other factors, such as weather, vegetation, and topography, that were not included in the analysis.

Further examining the performance of this model, Figure 4 shows the residuals plotted against the fitted values. The residuals were generally distributed above and below zero without a clear curved pattern, further indicating a linear relationship after the log transformations. The vertical groups of observations at the lower end occurred because time to containment was measured in whole days, causing many fires to have the same predictor value. Lastly, the spread of the residuals was not completely constant across the fitted values, particularly near the lower and upper ends of the plot. This indicates that the equal variance assumption was not fully met. Because of this, we have to question the reliability of our statistical inference. The unequal error variance can lead to inaccurate standard errors and, by extension, inaccurate confidence intervals and p-values.

```{r residuals-versus-fitted, fig.cap="Residuals plotted against fitted values for the regression model.", fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
plot(
  fitted(model),
  residuals(model),
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.4,
  col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.2),
  xlab = "Fitted Values",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  main = "Residuals versus Fitted Values"
)

abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Figure 5 demonstrates the normal quantile-quantile plot of the residuals. Most of the observations near the center of the distribution followed the reference line. However, the lower tail diverged from the fitted line, demonstrating that the residuals were not completely normally distributed. This indicates that some fires burned much less acreage than the model predicted. However, since the dataset contains a large number of observations, these departures are unlikely to negatively affect the overall regression line to a significant extent, but they should be considered when thinking about uncertainty.

```{r normal-qq-plot, fig.cap="Normal Q--Q plot of the regression residuals.", fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
qqnorm(
  residuals(model),
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.4,
  main = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals"
)

qqline(residuals(model), col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Overall, this analysis provides evidence of a positive association between time to containment and total area burned. In summary, longer containment durations were associated with larger fire perimeters, but containment duration was not enough to accurately predict the final size of every fire.

# Discussion

This analysis found a positive association between time to containment and total area burned by California wildfires. However, the model only explained about 24.57% of the variation. While longer containment durations were associated with larger fire perimeters, containment duration alone is not enough to accurately predict the final size of every fire.

I decided to include only data from 2000–2025, as this period provides a reasonable sample size for this project. While the dataset contains observations beginning in 1878, measurement technology from that time was not as precise and reliable as more recent technology.

All retained GIS-calculated acreage measurements were positive, so I applied the natural logarithm directly to acreage, including values between 0 and 1. These values produce negative logarithms, which are mathematically valid and do not require any additional adjustments.

These factors suggest that the validity and representativeness of the data are reasonably supported. The dataset includes wildfire perimeters collected by CAL FIRE and other cooperating agencies, making it relevant to our research question. In addition, since we are taking into account recorded wildfires within California in recent years, our sample covers a substantial portion of the population of interest. We are looking to make inferences about the relationship between containment duration and area burned for modern fires, so filtering our dataset to fires from 2000 onward is appropriate for our research question.

The residual vs. fitted plot showed no evident curved pattern, which supports the assumption of a linear relationship after transformation. However, the spread of the residuals was not equal, especially near the lower and upper fitted values, casting doubt on the equal error variance assumption. The Q-Q plot, showed a significant departure of normality within the lower tail. This leads us to reason that the equal variance and normality assumptions were not fully satisfied. Therefore our standard error, confidence intervals, and hypothesis test need to be interpreted with caution.

It is important to consider that while our results show an association, this does not establish a causal relationship. Additional factors that contribute to fire spread cannot be covered within the scope of this project. For example, the independence assumption may be violated because fires can be affected by overlapping environmental conditions or occur in similar spatial environments. If spatial or temporal dependencies exist, OLS standard errors may be underestimated, producing confidence intervals that are too narrow and p-values that are too small. Therefore, this model is only capable of measuring association.

The primary goal of this analysis is to describe the association between containment duration and area burned. Containment duration is not known until the fire has already been contained; therefore, it cannot be used as a predictor at the beginning of the fire’s active lifespan.
